article.title: Transgender Day of Remembrance — Why We Fight
article.author: DSA National Statements
article.content: [Content Warning – Violence and Suicide] This year, over 50* Transgender Americans have lost their lives due to societal violence. One of these is 29 year old Hailey Singleton from Dunnellon, who while living in Florida, was found along a dirt road with gunshot wounds. Davonta Curtis from Chicago, Illinois is one of the many BIPOC Trans people that are no longer with us. In Boise, Idaho, May Pollard is one of the three youngest people listed at 16 years old. She, along with Sydney Lou Walden from Lancaster, Pennsylvania, were one of at least 20 who committed suicide. On November 20th, crowds across the country are gathering for Transgender Day of Remembrance, where poets, priests and local politicians will speak about the plight of America’s (arguably) most marginalized and targeted minority for demonization by the American political establishment. Members of the community will talk about friends, family, brothers, sisters and siblings that have been lost to a society that has refused to accept them. Parents will mourn their children. Children will mourn their parents. The names of the dead will be remembered, and the community that rallies around them will collectively answer the question of why we fight — the names of those lost. In 2017, DSA’s Queer Socialist Working Group, now known as the Queer and Feminist Commission, argued that Trans people are scapegoated by conservatives as part of the barbaric process of creating the inequality that capitalism feeds on. Nine years later, we ask another question: How will we fight back against that barbarism? Our existence in society has been challenged at a fundamental level. Hostile investigations are launched, oftentimes victimizing gender non-conforming cis-women, when someone suspects a Transgender person has “Invaded” the “wrong bathroom”, demanding that the accused expose their body to satisfy investigators. After moving from Iowa to Minnesota, which has passed trans refuge laws, two Trans Minnesotans were attacked in public, with onlookers cheering on the assault. In this country, after being pushed to the ground during an onslaught of bigoted language, if one of us draws a weapon in clear self defense, we face felony charges and have our fundraiser campaigns for medical expenses suspended thanks to GoFundMe. Protections for Trans people against sexual abuse in prisons and ICE detentions centers have been eliminated . Gender identity is no longer a protected class to protect from discrimination in Iowa. Many of us are prohibited from updating our documentation to have the correct name and gender. In Kansas, chances are your documents were made invalid before you even had the opportunity to update them. It’s clear that this government has targeted us. Anyone who demeans our existence and regurgitates bigotry in the name of electability are not our allies. When they demand that we engage in the politics of assimilation and respectability, they are not our allies. Indiana’s soon to be Secretary of State Beau Bayh and Ohio’s soon-to-be Governor Amy Acton were two of many candidates that regurgitated anti-trans rhetoric by agreeing with statements like “we should not have men playing women’s sports,” suggesting they view Trans women as men. In Washington, Marie Gluesenkamp Perez won reelection handedly even after voting for a bill to out Trans students to parents. Josh Turek, the newly elected Democratic US Senator from Iowa, released an ad in the last few days of the election cycle to advocate for the ending of all federal funding for gender affirming care, which is a stance more harmful and transphobic than the Republican party has yet to suggest. With Democrats like these, who needs Republicans? Hostility towards Trans people has gained ground. At the same time, efforts to defend, support, and uplift the Trans community have only gotten stronger. To start, the anti-trans ballot measure in Missouri , which was linked to a potential abortion ban, was rejected by voters by an almost eleven point margin. And while the country was celebrating an electoral victory against our fascist government and its illegal wars, the Transgender community was rallying and protesting in the state capitols where the ballot measures were successful, like Arizona and Colorado, as they sought to undermine our right to exist. The fight against these ballot measures and for our dignity has been taken to court, with parents of transgender and cisgender students joining legal efforts to block the anti-trans sports ballot measure in Washington from going into effect. We’ve seen victories for trans rights in Virginia, New York and Seattle, as America’s Presidential administration walks back a rule that would have withheld federal funds for hospitals that provide gender affirming care for Trans youth. The midterms have seen a number of accomplices within the political establishment elected. Victoria Broderick, the US House Rep-elect from the fourth Congressional district in Tennessee come January specifically called out candidates speaking about Trans people in sports, saying that “any politician talking about men in women’s sports is a lazy politician.” US Senator-elect Abdul El Sayed from Michigan, has been a strong ally of trans rights. When pressed on the issue by Bari Weiss’ 60 Minutes he stated “I believe in rights. And even though somebody might use rights that you don’t understand, you never mean to use yourself, you still have to show up and fight for those rights.” What’s even more encouraging are the Democratic Socialists elected this cycle that are unapologetic and unfiltered with their support for Trans people. Such examples include Claire Valdez from New York City, who had a section on her policy page entitled “Queer and Trans Liberation,” and Melat Kiros from Denver, who displayed a “TRANS BILL OF RIGHTS” on hers. In the halls of power where our bodies have been legislated upon, our voices have been added to the conversation. From the South in Florida and Georgia, to the Midwest in Michigan, a sentiment starts to become unignorable: Your comfort does not justify silencing us, and we will not be silent in the face of bigotry against us. Jaelynn Scott, the second Democratic Socialist elected to Washington’s state legislature, the first Trans woman elected to Washington’s state legislature, and the first openly Trans Black woman elected to public office, had this to say about what these electoral victories meant. “Not only can we lead, but we can lead with power, with your brilliance, and our principles. We can lead proudly, as Black Trans women, as Trans women, as Trans men, as Non-Binary people, we can be ourselves. Let this win represent that to you and know that you can go as far as you want to. I got your back, and this community has your back.” We were not the first scapegoat for their barbarism, and we will not be the last. Only through a solidarity that unites all working people against this exploitative system can we be free. With recognition that the capitalist system must have a scapegoat, none of us are free until we are all free — until we reject the inherent bigotry of this system. Dear siblings — Get out and organize. If you can see these oppressions as linked, stand with the DSA to fight against all forms of inequality. A better world is possible, and Trans people will be liberated in that world. DSA Queer Feminist Commission and Trans Rights and Bodily Autonomy Campaign DSA National Political Committee *While many organizations may be referring to the number of Trans people that were victims of violence, we decided to use the number provided by Remembering Our Dead to account for the social, political, or economic systems that contribute to the premature death of Trans people. Even then, the number is likely higher than the one accounted for. The post Transgender Day of Remembrance — Why We Fight appeared first on Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) .
